title: CUET Mass Media Test 13
subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Mass Media - 318.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Mass Media papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: CBSE Mass Media Studies, Classes XI-XII (curriculum mirrored by the NTA syllabus)
Constitution of India, Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Acts and Supreme Court judgments as cited
Official histories of All India Radio, Doordarshan and Indian cinema
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a case; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: Because listeners cannot re-read what they hear, radio writers should use:
options: A) Long sentences packed with figures
B) Short sentences and everyday words
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Short sentences and everyday words
Why: Short sentences and simple words are easy to follow by ear.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) make listening harder.
Key point: Radio is written for the ear, not the eye.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: A small item that fills space
questions.question: A short news item used to fill a small gap on a page is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Filler
Why: A filler is a short item used to fill leftover space.
Why not the others: (A) is the main story. (B) is a longer human-interest piece. (D) is the paper's opinion.
Key point: Fillers help sub-editors complete a page.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: A shot of an eye filling the screen
questions.question: A shot in which a single eye fills the whole screen is called an:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Extreme close-up
Why: An extreme close-up shows a small detail in great size.
Why not the others: (B) shows the setting. (C) is filmed from behind one person. (D) shows a vast area.
Key point: Extreme close-ups add intensity.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: Gyan Vani, an FM radio network linked to IGNOU, was set up mainly for:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Education
Why: Gyan Vani was an educational FM network.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were not its main purpose.
Key point: Radio has long been used for distance education.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: The groups an organisation talks to
questions.question: In public relations, groups such as employees, customers, shareholders and neighbours are called the organisation's:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Publics
Why: Publics are the groups with whom an organisation must communicate.
Why not the others: (A) fund events. (B) are competitors. (D) are firms that provide services.
Key point: Different publics need different messages.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: How an agency tries to win a client
questions.question: An advertising agency's presentation of campaign ideas to win a new client is called a ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) pitch
Why: A pitch presents an agency's ideas to a prospective client.
Why not the others: (A) is the client's instructions to the agency. (C) is a short song. (D) is the arrangement of an ad.
Key point: Agencies compete for clients through pitches.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: The frequency of a radio station is measured in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Hertz
Why: Frequency is measured in hertz, usually kilohertz or megahertz for radio.
Why not the others: (B) measures power. (C) measures loudness. (D) measures electric potential.
Key point: An FM station's number, such as 93.5, is in megahertz.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Moving the camera during a shot
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Shot)
(A) Crane shot
(B) Tracking shot
(C) Handheld shot
(D) Steadicam shot

List-II (Effect)
(I) The camera rises high above the scene
(II) Smooth movement while the operator walks
(III) Moves alongside a moving subject, often on rails
(IV) A shaky look that feels immediate and real
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: A crane shot rises above the scene (I). A tracking shot moves alongside the subject (III). A handheld shot looks shaky and immediate (IV), and a Steadicam keeps moving shots smooth (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps crane and tracking. (B) swaps tracking and handheld. (D) swaps handheld and Steadicam.
Key point: Camera movement shapes how viewers feel.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: A program that appears useful but secretly harms the computer or steals data is called a ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Trojan horse
Why: A Trojan horse hides harmful code inside a program that looks harmless.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) protect computers. (C) is used to view web pages.
Key point: Download software only from trusted sources.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Unlike face-to-face talk, in mass communication:
options: A) Each receiver replies to the sender instantly
B) Feedback from receivers is delayed and indirect
C) The audience is small and known personally
D) No technology is needed to send messages
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Feedback from receivers is delayed and indirect
Why: Feedback in mass communication comes later and indirectly, for example through letters, ratings or comments.
Why not the others: (A) describes face-to-face talk. (C) is false; the audience is large and unknown. (D) is false; mass media rely on technology.
Key point: Delayed feedback separates mass communication from face-to-face talk.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: The person who handles the TV camera
questions.question: The person who operates the camera during a TV shoot is called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Camera operator
Why: The camera operator handles the camera and frames the shots.
Why not the others: (A) presents the show. (C) writes it. (D) prepares the performers' looks.
Key point: Camera operators follow the director's shot plan.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: Newspapers such as The Hindu and The Times of India, which come out every morning, are examples of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Dailies
Why: Papers published every day are called dailies.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) appear once a week, once in two weeks and once a month.
Key point: Dailies carry the latest news.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: The shape of the old TV screen
questions.question: The older, nearly square television screen had an aspect ratio of ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4:3
Why: Standard-definition TV used a 4:3 frame, which is almost square.
Why not the others: (A) is widescreen TV. (B) is ultra-wide cinema. (C) is a perfect square.
Key point: TV moved from 4:3 to 16:9 with widescreen and HD.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: Which of the following is the strongest password?
options: B) your own date of birth
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) tR7#mQ!2vL9x
Why: A long mix of capital and small letters, numbers and symbols is hardest to guess.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are common or personal and easy to guess.
Key point: Strong, unique passwords protect accounts.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: A newspaper office in another city
questions.question: A newspaper's office in a city other than its main office, staffed by reporters, is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bureau
Why: A bureau is a branch news office.
Why not the others: (B) is the paper's archive. (C) carries the paper's name. (D) is a page plan.
Key point: Bureaus let papers cover news from many places.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question: Saving photos and documents on remote servers over the internet, so they can be reached from any device, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cloud storage
Why: Cloud storage keeps files on internet servers that can be reached from anywhere.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) keep files on one's own device or drive. (C) erases a disk.
Key point: The cloud supports convergence across devices.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Information Technology Act, 2000:
(A) Section 66C punishes identity theft, such as misusing another person's password.
(B) Section 66D punishes cheating by impersonation using a computer.
(C) Section 67 punishes publishing obscene material in electronic form.
(D) Section 66A is still in force against offensive online messages.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct descriptions of these sections.
Why not the others: (D) is false. The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A in Shreya Singhal (2015). Options (C) and (D) include (D), and (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Cyber law punishes specific harms, not vague offence.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question: In James Grunig's models of PR, the two-way symmetrical model aims at:
options: A) Spreading publicity without checking facts
B) Giving out information in one direction only
C) Persuading publics using research about them
D) Mutual understanding through dialogue with publics
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mutual understanding through dialogue with publics
Why: The two-way symmetrical model uses dialogue so that both the organisation and its publics may change.
Why not the others: (A) is press agentry. (B) is the public information model. (C) is the two-way asymmetrical model.
Key point: Grunig saw dialogue as the most ethical form of PR.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Reality shows are fully scripted dramas performed by trained actors.
(B) A docudrama recreates real events, often with actors.
(C) A talk show is built around a host and guests.
(D) In a game show, contestants compete for prizes.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false. Reality shows feature ordinary people in unscripted situations, though they are edited.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Each format has its own conventions.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) VSNL launches public internet service in India
(B) ARPANET links its first computers
(C) Facebook is launched
(D) Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: ARPANET began in 1969 and the Web was proposed in 1989. VSNL opened public internet in India in 1995, and Facebook began in 2004.
Why not the others: (A) puts 1989 before 1969. (C) puts 1995 before 1989. (D) puts 2004 before 1995.
Key point: The internet took decades to become a mass medium.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps of producing an investigative story in the correct order:
(A) Publish the story
(B) Receive a tip-off about possible wrongdoing
(C) Seek a response from the people accused
(D) Collect documents and other evidence
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (C), (A)
Why: The journalist gets a tip-off, gathers evidence, asks the accused for their side, and only then publishes.
Why not the others: (A) gathers evidence before the tip. (C) seeks a response before gathering evidence. (D) publishes before seeking a response.
Key point: Fairness demands that the accused be heard before publication.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: The scholar who shaped communication studies
questions.question: ____ is often called the father of communication studies.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Wilbur Schramm
Why: Wilbur Schramm set up some of the first communication research programmes and is often called the father of communication studies.
Why not the others: (B) is known for "the medium is the message". (C) gave the SMCR model. (D) gave the verbal "who says what" model.
Key point: Schramm made communication a field of study.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps of recording a radio interview in the correct order:
(A) Edit out mistakes and long pauses
(B) Broadcast the edited interview
(C) Do a test to set the sound level
(D) Record the interview
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: The producer sets the level, records the interview, edits it, and then broadcasts it.
Why not the others: (A) records before the level test. (B) edits before recording. (D) broadcasts before editing.
Key point: A level check prevents distorted or faint recordings.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad started the Urdu weekly ____ in 1912.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Al-Hilal
Why: Azad launched Al-Hilal in Calcutta in 1912 to rouse nationalist feeling.
Why not the others: (B) was Tilak's paper. (C) and (D) were associated with Gandhi.
Key point: Papers in many languages carried the freedom movement.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Culture once seen as belonging to an elite
questions.question: Classical music, opera and fine art, traditionally associated with a small educated class, are described as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) High culture
Why: High culture refers to art forms traditionally valued by an educated elite.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are enjoyed by large numbers of people. (B) is the traditional culture of communities.
Key point: Mass media have blurred the line between high and popular culture.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: The ability to access, analyse and evaluate media messages is called ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) media literacy
Why: Media literacy helps people question and judge what they see, hear and read.
Why not the others: (A) is the merging of media. (B) is the dominance of foreign media. (C) is who owns media firms.
Key point: Media literacy protects audiences from manipulation.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Lasswell's model is stated as a set of questions: who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect.
(B) In the Osgood–Schramm model, each participant both encodes and decodes messages.
(C) Shannon and Weaver's model was first developed for telephone engineering.
(D) The Westley–MacLean model has no place for a gatekeeper.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false. The Westley–MacLean model includes a gatekeeper, such as an editor, who selects messages for the audience.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Each model highlights a different part of communication.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Element)
(A) Banner headline
(B) Jump line
(C) Standfirst
(D) Pull quote

List-II (Description)
(I) Tells readers where a story continues, such as "Continued on page 7"
(II) A striking line from the story printed large to catch the eye
(III) A headline running across the full width of the page
(IV) A short summary printed between the headline and the story
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: A banner headline spans the page (III). A jump line says where a story continues (I). A standfirst summarises the story under the headline (IV), and a pull quote enlarges a striking line (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps banner and jump line. (B) swaps jump line and standfirst. (D) swaps standfirst and pull quote.
Key point: Page elements guide the reader through a story.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and advertising
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
(A) It set up the Central Consumer Protection Authority.
(B) The Authority can act against false or misleading advertisements.
(C) A celebrity who endorses a misleading advertisement can be penalised.
(D) The Act covers print advertisements only, not online ones.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. The Authority can order misleading advertisements to stop and can penalise makers and endorsers.
Why not the others: (D) is false. The Act applies to advertisements in all media, including online. Options (C) and (D) include (D), and (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Endorsers share responsibility for the claims they promote.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: What the word "copy" means in a newsroom
questions.question: In a newsroom, the word "copy" refers to:
options: A) A photocopy of an official document
B) A story copied from another paper
C) The written text of a news story
D) The number of copies printed each day
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The written text of a news story
Why: Copy is the written material that reporters file and editors check.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not what the term means in a newsroom.
Key point: Copy editors check copy before it is printed.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Advertising)
(A) Pioneering advertising
(B) Competitive advertising
(C) Advocacy advertising
(D) Reminder advertising

List-II (Purpose)
(I) Keeps a well-known brand in people's minds
(II) Takes a stand on a public issue
(III) Persuades buyers to choose one brand over its rivals
(IV) Creates demand for a new kind of product
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Pioneering advertising creates demand for a new kind of product (IV). Competitive advertising promotes one brand over rivals (III). Advocacy advertising takes a stand on an issue (II), and reminder advertising keeps a known brand in mind (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps pioneering and competitive. (C) swaps competitive and advocacy. (D) swaps advocacy and reminder.
Key point: An advertisement's purpose changes as a product matures.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: A teacher explaining a lesson aloud in class is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Oral communication
Why: Oral communication uses spoken words.
Why not the others: (A) uses writing. (B) uses gestures and expressions. (D) uses images.
Key point: Oral communication allows quick clarification.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: The people a campaign wants to reach
questions.question: The particular group of people an advertising campaign is designed to reach is its:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Target audience
Why: The target audience is the group the campaign aims at.
Why not the others: (A) is the set of media used. (B) is the money available. (C) is a memorable line.
Key point: Every campaign begins with knowing its audience.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about documentary films:
(A) An expository documentary uses a narrator to explain a subject or argument.
(B) Historical documentaries often use archival footage.
(C) A documentary may never use background music.
(D) A documentary may combine interviews, actuality and narration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Documentaries use narration, archive material, interviews and real footage in many combinations.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Many documentaries use music to set mood. Options (B) and (D) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Documentary has many forms, all rooted in real material.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question: A book published in digital form to be read on a phone, tablet or e-reader is called an:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) E-book
Why: An e-book is a digital version of a book.
Why not the others: (A) is read aloud and recorded. (B) is a yearly reference book. (D) is a collection of writings.
Key point: E-books are part of the shift to digital media.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: What does not make an event newsworthy
questions.question: An editor is choosing stories for tomorrow's paper. Which of these should NOT decide whether an event is news?
options: C) Prominence of the people involved
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The reporter's own liking
Why: News values are qualities of an event, such as being recent, nearby or about well-known people. A reporter's personal liking is not one.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are recognised news values.
Key point: News values help editors choose stories fairly.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: Short, vertical videos shared on Instagram are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Reels
Why: Reels are Instagram's short-video format.
Why not the others: (A) disappear after 24 hours. (B) are linked text posts. (C) are audio programmes.
Key point: Short video now dominates social media.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Four newspapers in the order they appeared
questions.question:
Arrange the following newspapers in the order in which they were first published:
(A) Kesari
(B) Samachar Darpan
(C) Young India
(D) Bombay Samachar
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: Samachar Darpan appeared in 1818 and Bombay Samachar in 1822. Kesari followed in 1881, and Gandhi's Young India in 1919.
Why not the others: (B) puts 1822 before 1818. (C) puts 1881 before 1822. (D) puts 1919 before 1881.
Key point: The Indian press grew from the early 1800s into a voice of the freedom movement.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: A task an ad agency does not do
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of an advertising agency?
options: A) Printing the newspaper in which the ad appears
B) Writing the copy and designing the visuals
C) Planning and buying space and time in the media
D) Researching consumers and the market
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Printing the newspaper in which the ad appears
Why: The newspaper prints itself. The agency creates the advertisement and buys space in it.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are core agency functions.
Key point: Agencies create and place advertisements.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Element of Berlo's model)
(A) Source
(B) Message
(C) Channel
(D) Receiver

List-II (Example of what it includes)
(I) The five senses: hearing, seeing, touching, smelling, tasting
(II) The sender's communication skills, attitudes and knowledge
(III) The listener's own skills, attitudes and knowledge
(IV) Content, code and treatment
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: In Berlo's model the source has skills, attitudes and knowledge (II). The message has content, code and treatment (IV). The channel works through the five senses (I), and the receiver has their own skills and attitudes (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps source and message. (C) swaps message and channel. (D) swaps channel and receiver.
Key point: Berlo stressed that sender and receiver must share skills and attitudes.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Format)
(A) Listicle
(B) News quiz
(C) Slideshow
(D) Long-form article

List-II (Description)
(I) Interactive questions that test readers on the week's news
(II) An in-depth narrative piece that takes time to read
(III) A series of pictures that readers click through
(IV) An article written as a numbered list
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: A listicle is a numbered list (IV). A news quiz is interactive (I). A slideshow is a set of pictures (III), and a long-form article is in-depth (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps listicle and quiz. (B) swaps quiz and slideshow. (C) swaps slideshow and long-form.
Key point: Digital news uses many formats to engage readers.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Feature)
(A) Hashtag
(B) Mention
(C) Repost
(D) Handle

List-II (Use)
(I) A user's name on a platform, such as @newsdesk
(II) Shares someone else's post with one's own followers
(III) Labels a post by topic so others can find it
(IV) Tags another user in a post so that they are notified
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: A hashtag labels a topic (III). A mention tags a user (IV). A repost shares another's post (II), and a handle is a username (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps hashtag and mention. (C) swaps mention and repost. (D) swaps repost and handle.
Key point: These features help posts spread and connect users.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: The Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023:
(A) It replaced the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867.
(B) Registration under it is handled by the Press Registrar General of India.
(C) Books continue to be registered under this Act.
(D) It provides for registering periodicals online.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. The 2023 Act replaced the colonial-era law and made registration of periodicals simpler and online.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Books were taken out of the scope of the new Act. Options (B) and (C) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: The 2023 Act updated a law that was over 150 years old.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: A reporter based in another country
questions.question: A journalist posted in another country to report from there is called a foreign ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) correspondent
Why: A foreign correspondent is based abroad and reports news from that country.
Why not the others: (A) writes regular opinion pieces. (C) edits copy. (D) checks typeset text.
Key point: Foreign correspondents bring world news to readers.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Station ID
(B) Filler
(C) Time check
(D) Sign-off

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A short item used to fill spare air time
(II) An announcement of the station's name and frequency
(III) The closing announcement at the end of the day's broadcast
(IV) The presenter tells listeners the time
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: A station ID gives the station's name and frequency (II). A filler fills spare time (I). A time check tells the time (IV), and a sign-off closes the day's broadcast (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps station ID and filler. (B) swaps filler and time check. (C) swaps time check and sign-off.
Key point: Small on-air routines keep listeners oriented.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: The Grand Café show of December 1895
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

For a film club screening, Ananya prepares a talk on how cinema began. She starts in Paris on 28 December 1895, when the Lumière brothers showed a set of short films to a paying audience at the Grand Café. Each film was under a minute long and was shot with a fixed camera. They showed everyday scenes just as they happened, such as workers leaving a factory and a train pulling into a station. The Lumières' Cinématographe could record, print and project films. Within a year, Lumière operators had screened films in Bombay.

She then turns to Robert Flaherty, who lived for months with an Inuit family in the Canadian Arctic before completing Nanook of the North (1922). The film follows Nanook and his family through their daily struggle to survive, but some scenes, such as an old-style hunt, were staged for the camera.

In 1926 the Scottish film-maker John Grierson, reviewing Flaherty's next film, Moana, used the word "documentary". He later defined documentary as "the creative treatment of actuality". Grierson went on to lead government film units in Britain that made films for public education.

Question: The Lumière show at the Grand Café in Paris in December 1895 is remembered as:
options: A) An early public film show for a paying audience
B) The first Indian film ever to be screened
C) The first film to be made with sound
D) The first colour film shown in a cinema
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) An early public film show for a paying audience
Why: The Lumière brothers' screening for a paying public in Paris in 1895 is widely taken as the start of cinema as a public show.
Why not the others: (B) Indian film-making began later, in 1913. (C) Sound films came in the late 1920s. (D) Early films were black and white.
Key point: Cinema began as a public show of short films.

Question: The Lumière films of workers and a train are called "actualities" because they:
options: A) Told invented stories with trained actors
B) Recorded real everyday scenes as they happened
C) Used drawings brought to life frame by frame
D) Were made only to advertise factory products
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Recorded real everyday scenes as they happened
Why: Actualities were short films that simply recorded real scenes of everyday life.
Why not the others: (A) describes fiction films. (C) describes animation. (D) is not why they are called actualities.
Key point: The first films were records of real life.

Question: Some scenes in Nanook of the North were staged for the camera. This raises which question about documentary film?
options: A) Whether documentaries should be shot in colour
B) Whether documentaries need a written script at all
C) How far events may be recreated while staying truthful
D) Whether documentaries can be shown in cinemas
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) How far events may be recreated while staying truthful
Why: Staging scenes makes viewers ask how much a documentary may reconstruct events and still claim to show reality.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not raised by the staging of scenes.
Key point: Reconstruction is a long-debated issue in documentary.

questions.sub_topic: Grierson's idea of treating actuality creatively
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

For a film club screening, Ananya prepares a talk on how cinema began. She starts in Paris on 28 December 1895, when the Lumière brothers showed a set of short films to a paying audience at the Grand Café. The Lumières' Cinématographe could record, print and project films. Within a year, Lumière operators had screened films in Bombay.

She then turns to Robert Flaherty, who lived for months with an Inuit family in the Canadian Arctic before completing Nanook of the North (1922). The film follows Nanook and his family through their daily struggle to survive, but some scenes, such as an old-style hunt, were staged for the camera.

Question: Grierson's definition of documentary as "the creative treatment of actuality" means that a documentary:
options: A) Must be shot and shown without any editing at all
B) Invents its events and characters, as a feature film does
C) Must avoid music, narration and graphics of every kind
D) Shapes real material through selection and editing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Shapes real material through selection and editing
Why: A documentary is built from real people and events, but the film-maker shapes this material by choosing, ordering and editing it.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are false; documentaries are edited and often use music and narration. (B) describes fiction.
Key point: Documentary is reality shaped by a point of view.

Question: Which of the following best states how Nanook of the North moved beyond the Lumière actualities?
options: A) It shaped real life into a long story built around one family
B) It was the first film ever projected before a paying public
C) It used professional actors in place of real people
D) It was shot in a studio, unlike the Lumière films
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It shaped real life into a long story built around one family
Why: The Lumière films recorded single short scenes. Flaherty followed real people over a long film and shaped their life into a story.
Why not the others: (B) was the Lumière show of 1895. (C) is false; Nanook used real Inuit people. (D) is false; it was shot in the Arctic.
Key point: Flaherty added storytelling to the recording of reality.
